result:
The window does not sleep, but it does forget. Every morning, light returns like a familiar stranger, and the glass remembers—briefly—that it is not a wall but a membrane, a thin negotiation between inside and out.

Consider the dust. It settles not out of neglect, but out of loyalty. Each particle is a small record of breath, of rain that never quite reached the sill, of the distant factory whose smoke turned gold in the late autumn sun. The window collects these things without judgment. It has no opinion on the storm that rattles its frame, nor on the quiet Tuesday when nothing happens except a single fly tracing the geometry of the pane. It witnesses. That is its only vocation.

We call this transparency a virtue, as if seeing through something makes it less real. But the window knows otherwise. To be seen through is not to be invisible; it is to be indispensable. Without it, the room is a cave. With it, the room becomes a thought that includes the sky.

There is a particular hour—just before dusk—when the glass stops reflecting and starts glowing from within, not because a lamp has been lit, but because the world outside has dimmed enough to let the interior claim its own light. In that hour, the window is neither entrance nor exit. It is a question suspended in space: *What separates you from what you love?* And the answer, always temporary, is: very little. Only a layer of sand turned to clarity, only the decision to stay open.

So let the rain come. Let it stripe the view with its brief, vertical handwriting. The window will hold it for a moment, then let it go. That is the nature of being a boundary that refuses to divide—receiving everything, keeping nothing, and in that refusal, becoming exactly what it was made to be.
